claims.text: Extremely rapid heating and cooling kinetically stabilizes a single-phase solid solution in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid temperature cycling suppresses precursor mobility and elemental diffusion.
Inhibition of precursor mobility favors stochastic formation of a single-phase alloy nanoparticle.
A brief exposure at high temperature limits diffusion of the individual metallic species.
Extending the high-temperature dwell time increases elemental diffusion.
The additional diffusion produced by an extended dwell triggers thermodynamically driven elemental segregation.
The additional diffusion produced by an extended dwell transforms the initially single phase into secondary or mixed phases.
Rapid processing of the precursor mixture can produce a disordered single-phase solid-solution nanoparticle.
The rapidly processed baseline nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
The proposed regime applies to noble metal–based nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
The applicable peak-temperature range is approximately 1100–2000 K.
The applicable rapid-cooling range is approximately 10^4–10^5 K/s.
The synthesis regime uses an inert atmosphere such as argon.
An extended high-temperature dwell will produce detectable secondary crystalline phases relative to the rapid-processing baseline.
An extended high-temperature dwell will produce detectable elemental inhomogeneity relative to the baseline.
An extended high-temperature dwell may change nanoparticle morphology.
The critical dwell time for observable phase separation varies with elemental combination and diffusion kinetics.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that any controlled extension of the high-temperature dwell triggers phase separation, whereas the mechanism requires sufficient diffusion and the uncertainty field acknowledges an unknown critical dwell time. These latter statements imply a threshold rather than an effect from any extension.
